analysis.one_liner: Takes congressional map-drawing away from state politicians and gives it to independent commissions.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or a House floor vote and died at the end of the 116th Congress with only 2 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require every state to draw its congressional districts through an independent commission instead of letting the state legislature do it. Commissions could not consider voters' party affiliation, voting history, or where incumbents live, could only redistrict once per census unless a court orders otherwise, and would have to hold public meetings, post data online, and let anyone submit their own map. If a state failed to act, state or federal courts would draw the map instead.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters, whose districts are currently drawn by the same state politicians who have an interest in keeping their own seats safe. The bill bans the commission from considering party affiliation, voting history, or incumbents' home addresses, requires open public meetings and an online tool anyone can use to draft and submit maps, and limits each state to one redistricting after each census unless a court orders another one to comply with the Constitution or the Voting Rights Act.

how_it_helps.text: Districts would be drawn by a commission whose members are barred from having held office, run for office, or worked for a party or candidate in the prior four years, and who must pledge not to run for Congress until after the next apportionment.

The commission may not consider voting history or party affiliation (except as needed to comply with the Voting Rights Act or a state competitive-district law) or the residence of incumbent House members.

A state may not be redistricted more than once after each census unless a court orders a second redistricting to comply with the Constitution or enforce the Voting Rights Act, curbing mid-decade remaps for partisan advantage.

Commissions must hold public meetings, post census and voting data with interactive mapping software, accept public map submissions and comments, and publish district maps and dissents before submitting a plan.

If a commission's plan is not enacted, the state's highest court may choose among commission-drafted plans, and a U.S. district court must draw the map if the state court declines or the state never creates a commission — so the legislature cannot simply block reform.

analysis.who_pays: Incumbent House members and the majority parties in state legislatures, who lose control over the maps that protect their seats. The only public money involved is a federal payment of $150,000 per congressional seat to run each state's commission, paid out of federal appropriations.
analysis.who_pays_short: Incumbent politicians and state party leaders

drawbacks.text: Commission members are still appointed by the majority and minority leaders of the state legislature's upper and lower chambers, so the people who run the statehouse retain a hand in choosing who draws the maps.

The bill preempts traditional state control over congressional redistricting under the Constitution's Elections Clause approach it cites, a federalism change critics would contest, and states that fail to create a commission would have a federal district court draw their maps.
The federal payment of $150,000 per congressional seat is an authorization of appropriations with no fixed cap on total cost, and states with only one representative get no payment at all.
Members appointed by state legislative leaders could still serve their appointers' interests even though they cannot have been officials themselves.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to voters — districts that can no longer be engineered around party affiliation or incumbents' addresses, with one map per census and a public process — outweighs the costs, which are mostly the federal money to run commissions and the transfer of a power states have held for two centuries. The biggest design weakness is that legislative leaders still appoint the commissioners, though the eligibility rules and ban on party-based line-drawing limit how much that matters.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced, then to its Constitution subcommittee, and never received a markup or a floor vote before the 116th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Cohen introduced the bill on January 3, 2019, the first day of the 116th Congress, and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee.
The same day it was referred to the Subcommittee on the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties, and no further action is recorded in the bill's history.
Only two House members cosponsored the bill, both Democrats, and neither the full committee nor the House ever voted on it.

The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and the bill died without a vote; a similar measure had not advanced either, and redistricting remained under state legislative control for the post-2020 census maps.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent House members and the majority parties in state legislatures kept the power to draw their own congressional districts after the 2020 census — the outcome the bill would have changed. Voters in states with aggressive partisan maps got no relief.

for.name: Rep. Steve Cohen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and named it for former Rep. John Tanner, a retired Tennessee Democrat who had sponsored similar redistricting reform.

for.name: Reps. Sheila Jackson Lee and Eric Swalwell
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only cosponsors.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Constitution subcommittee on the day of introduction and never scheduled a markup or committee vote in two years.

against.name: House Democratic leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor despite Democrats holding 231 of 429 seats.

against.name: Incumbent House members and state legislative majorities of both parties
against.what_they_did: Drew the post-2020 congressional maps under existing state control, preserving the system the bill would have replaced.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever recorded; the only support shown in the record was 2 Democratic cosponsors out of 231 House Democrats, with no Republican cosponsors.

industries.industry: Incumbent members of Congress and state legislative majority parties
industries.note: They currently draw congressional maps under state law, which the bill would move to citizen commissions barred from considering party or incumbents' homes. Losing that power is the direct cost of the bill's benefit to voters.
States lose exclusive authority over congressional redistricting and must create commissions to qualify for federal payments of $150,000 per seat. States with one representative receive nothing.
